tier_reason: First-party GB/s figures appear only as code comments in mem.h (said to be read off Intel PCM in real time); no harness, timing code, CPU model, compiler or flags, so C.

corrections.baseline: MSVC compiler-intrinsic memcpy and memset (the gist declares #pragma intrinsic(memcpy) and #pragma intrinsic(memset), i.e. the compiler/CRT built-ins), single-threaded and also run multithreaded; MSVC version not stated
corrections.claimed_speedup: Code comments: 'intrinsic memcpy (single threaded) at 22 GB/s', 'intrinsic memcpy (multithreaded) at 29 GB/s', '___memcpy_threaded at 33.3 GB/s (memory bandwidth is saturated)'; ___memset_threaded 'has the same 33.3 GB/s, but in this case it's all write bandwidth'. The 33.3 GB/s for memcpy is a combined figure ('read 10 GB/s + write 23.3 GB/s'). About 1.5x over the single-threaded intrinsic and about 1.15x over the multithreaded intrinsic (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Numbers are code comments from the author, measured as memory-controller traffic with Intel PCM, with no CPU model, compiler, flags, buffer size or harness. The baseline is MSVC's intrinsic memcpy/memset (#pragma intrinsic), not a custom routine. The 33.3 GB/s memcpy figure is read plus write bus traffic (10 + 23.3 GB/s), so it is not bytes-copied throughput, and it is unclear whether the 22 and 29 GB/s baseline figures were counted the same way; streaming stores also avoid read-for-ownership traffic, which changes what bus GB/s means. Against the fair multithreaded-intrinsic row the gain is only about 1.15x (derived from page data). The '16x faster' line about SSE stores over rep stosb is quoted from a Microsoft MSRC blog post, not measured. The header is not standalone: it includes the author's ..\Math\superfastmath.h, uses TBB parallel_for and PrefetchVirtualMemory without including their headers, and ___prefetch_vmem is never called (a commenter noted this). Windows/MSVC only (__declspec, __vectorcall), AVX2 streaming intrinsics. Four revisions, all June 10-12, 2022; the June 10, 2025 'last active' date is a comment, not a code change. Licence CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial, not OSI) next to an 'All Rights Reserved' copyright line.

notes: Numbers match the gist comments. Fixed the baseline description (it is MSVC's intrinsic memcpy/memset, not the author's own routine) and the last-change date (last revision 2022-06-12, so abandoned); the 2025 date was a comment. Shortcomings: comment-only numbers from PCM bus traffic, no CPU/compiler, only about 1.15x over a multithreaded intrinsic, non-commercial licence, header not standalone.

reject_reason: other: wrong-answer fast path and known project. The only row AssemblyScript wins (factorial) compares an i32 AssemblyScript factorial that overflows at 20 (returns -2102132736) against a JavaScript factorial that computes the exact 20! in float64; every row that computes the same thing shows AssemblyScript slower or tied. The page is also an evidence page for AssemblyScript (https://github.com/assemblyscript/assemblyscript, wave 12, tier D), whose caveats already cite these LeanyLabs results.
tier_reason: Code (benchmarks.js, assembly/index.ts), asc 0.18.4 with -O3 release flags (asconfig.json, package-lock.json) and the i5-8250 CPU are public, but the Node/V8 version that JIT-compiles both sides is not stated, and the one winning row compares different computations, so no valid number shows AssemblyScript faster.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: asc 0.18.4 (pinned in package-lock.json) release target in asconfig.json: optimizeLevel 3, shrinkLevel 0, converge, noAssert; benchmark.js 2.1.4; Node version not stated
corrections.caveats: AssemblyScript wins one of six workloads, ties one and loses four. The one win is invalid as a speed comparison: assembly/index.ts defines factorial(i: i32): i32, so factorial(20) wraps around and returns -2102132736, while benchmarks.js's factorialJs returns the exact 2432902008176640000 in float64 (past 13! V8 leaves small-integer arithmetic for doubles); the harness never checks results. 2021 numbers on AssemblyScript 0.18.4 and an unnamed Node version on an i5-8250 (U suffix missing in the README). One commit ('improve and normalize') came from MaxGraey, an AssemblyScript core developer. Five commits, the last on 2021-02-07.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly. Reject on the stb-zip/fast_resize precedent: the factorial win comes from wrapping i32 arithmetic that returns a wrong value, compared against JavaScript computing the right one. Otherwise JavaScript wins 4 of 6 and ties 1. If the orchestrator prefers to keep it, record it as a duplicate of the wave-12 AssemblyScript entry, which already cites this repo.

tier_reason: Independent measurement by the mathjs maintainer (discussion #2744, December 11, 2024) using public benchmark code (mathjs commit 7f02ba2, test/benchmark/matrix_operations.js, tinybench 3.0.7, eigen 0.2.2 from npm). The README documents emcc -O3 build flags, but no hardware or Node version is stated, so not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt npm package eigen 0.2.2 (Emscripten/embind build of an Eigen 3.3.9 subset); the README's build line is emcc -O3 -s ASSERTIONS=0 -s DISABLE_EXCEPTION_CATCHING=0 -s ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1 -s MODULARIZE=1 --bind (optionally -D NO_OSQP), but nothing confirms that the published package was built that way; benchmark: mathjs 14.0.0 at commit 7f02ba2, tinybench 3.0.7 with time 100 ms, Node version not stated
corrections.workload: mathjs test/benchmark/matrix_operations.js (tinybench, 100 ms per task): A+A, A*A, A' (transpose) and det(A) on a 25x25 Fiedler matrix, eigen-js vs mathjs (number and generic), sylvester, numeric.js and ndarray in Node.js.
corrections.caveats: Run by the mathjs maintainer in a GitHub discussion (December 11, 2024); machine and Node version are not stated; the matrix is 25x25 (Fiedler, set in the benchmark code). The maintainer says eigen-js is not an order of magnitude faster across the board: ndarray beats it on transpose and determinant (det 1.09 us vs 3.96 us), numeric.js on addition and transpose, and eigen-js ran out of memory until he worked around it. The harness never frees eigen-js results (each matAdd/matMul/transpose allocates a new wasm-heap matrix with no delete() or GC.flush()), so the timings exclude deallocation and the leak explains the out-of-memory errors. Tiny 25x25 inputs mostly measure call and allocation overhead. The eigen-js README itself makes no performance claim; last commit 2023-07-17.

notes: Numbers match the discussion exactly (A*A 5.31 vs 29.24 us, det 3.96 vs 218.70 us, A+A 2.21 vs 5.14 us, transpose 2.58 vs 2.49 us). Maintenance corrected to stale (last commit 2023-07-17, about 2.2 years ago). Possible duplicate: eigen-js is an Emscripten/embind JS wrapper of Eigen (https://gitlab.com/libeigen/eigen, wave0-seed); under the wrapper rule the orchestrator may record it as a duplicate.
